headline: FIFA drops World Cup sell-off plan
summary: FIFA scrapped a plan to sell private stakes in a new commercial arm holding its tournaments, and Wales became the first association to withdraw support for Infantino's re-election.
display_body: FIFA scrapped its most contentious commercial project in years, and its Swiss president, Gianni Infantino, ended the week fighting to keep his job. On 31 July, football's Zurich-based world governing body abandoned a plan — unveiled only days earlier, on 28 July — to move its tournaments into a new commercial company, FIFA Forward Enterprises (FFE), and sell a minority stake (reported at up to 21%) to private investors to raise around $4 billion for its 211 member associations. The revolt was near-total: UEFA said all 55 of its European members would oppose it, CONCACAF's 41 members formally rejected it too, and by FIFA's own admission the scheme had "fractured" the game and was no longer viable — so it was killed before any vote. The backlash then turned personal: days later the Football Association of Wales became the first member association to publicly withdraw its support for Infantino's re-election, citing failures of "governance, leadership and judgement," with other associations weighing similar moves.
why: Selling equity in the World Cup would have handed private financiers a lasting claim on football's most valuable asset. The opposition — spanning well over half of FIFA's 211 members — and Infantino's rare, humiliating U-turn are the clearest limit yet on how far the sport's Zurich power centre can commercialise the game over its members' objections.

headline: Young Boys and Lugano lead Super League
summary: Young Boys, Lugano and St. Gallen all won their opening two Swiss Super League matches; reigning champions Thun were thrashed 6-0.
display_body: Switzerland's new Super League season is two rounds old and already has a clear pacesetting group: Young Boys, Lugano and St. Gallen have all won both their games. Young Boys — the Bern club that are the competition's record champions — underlined their intent by thrashing last season's fairytale winners Thun 6-0, after opening with a 4-2 win over Sion; Lugano came from a goal down to win 4-1 at Grasshoppers. The early stumbles came from the bigger names: Basel, one of the country's traditional heavyweights, lost 1-0 at Lausanne, while Servette and Luzern both sit pointless after two games. It is far too soon to read a title race — the Swiss top flight runs to next May — but the opening fortnight has already inverted last season's order, with reigning champions Thun among those chasing.
why: In a league where a handful of clubs usually dominate, seeing last year's surprise champions hammered and a traditional power beaten inside the first two weekends is a reminder of how unsettled — and open — the Swiss title picture is heading into the autumn.

headline: Tour de France Femmes opens in Switzerland
summary: The Tour de France Femmes ran its first two stages in Switzerland; Lorena Wiebes won both to take yellow, with Swiss rider Noemi Ruegg fourth overall.
display_body: The Tour de France Femmes — the biggest race in women's cycling — began this year on Swiss roads, with its first two stages run entirely in Switzerland before the race crossed into France. Dutch sprinter Lorena Wiebes (SD Worx-Protime) dominated the Grand Départ, winning both the opening stage into Lausanne and Sunday's run from Aigle — home of cycling's world governing body, the UCI — along Lake Geneva, and she leads the general classification (the overall time standings) by 14 seconds. The Swiss interest is real: Noemi Rüegg (EF Education-Oatly) climbed to fourth overall, best of the home riders, while Marlen Reusser (Movistar) — one of the world's finest time-triallists (specialists in solo races against the clock) — crashed on stage two but rejoined the main group and sits in a cluster of favourites 20 seconds back. With mountain stages and a time trial still to come in France, the fight for the overall title has barely started.
why: A sprinter in yellow after two flat stages is normal; what matters for a non-follower is that the real contenders are still bunched within 20 seconds, so the race is wide open — and that a Swiss rider is sitting inside the top four as it heads for the decisive terrain.

headline: Australia top slimmed-down Glasgow Games
summary: Australia topped the medal table as a pared-back, roughly ten-sport Commonwealth Games closed in Glasgow on 2 August.
display_body: Australia comfortably topped the medal table as the Commonwealth Games closed in Glasgow on 2 August, finishing with roughly 70 golds and about 170 medals in all — well clear of England, second on around 110 medals, and Canada in third. The bigger story was the event itself: this was a deliberately pared-back Games, cut to about ten sports across a handful of venues after the Australian state of Victoria abandoned its hosting deal in 2023 and Glasgow stepped in to stop the Commonwealth Games collapsing entirely. Organisers called the compact model a success and a template for a cheaper future; sceptics counter that a single-city, ten-sport edition still leaves unanswered whether a 90-plus-nation event rooted in the British Empire has a lasting place on the modern sporting calendar. (Switzerland, not a Commonwealth country, does not compete.)
why: This was less a contest than a survival exercise for one of world sport's oldest multi-sport events — and it worked, but only by shrinking. The question it leaves is whether "smaller and cheaper" is a genuine future or just a stay of execution.
